title: Mid-term: linked list exam problems
overview: Module 12 is the mid-term exam of Basic Data Structures. The five questions test what you built in Modules 8-11: inserting at any index of a doubly linked list, printing it both ways, checking a palindrome with two pointers, a browser-history style walk, and query processing with the STL `list`. Each question has Shammunul's solution plus a `_p` practice re-type.

concepts.explain: Several questions end the input with `-1` (or the word `end`). Read in a `while(true)` loop and `break` when you see it, instead of reading a count first.
`sort()` orders a `list` in place and `unique()` removes **neighbouring** equal values. Sort first, then `unique()`, and every duplicate is gone.
Valid indexes are `0..size`. Index `0` is insert-at-head, index `size` is insert-at-tail, anything in between needs the node before the position and four pointer updates.
Forward printing follows `next` from `head`; backward printing follows `prev` from `tail`. If the backward line looks wrong, a `prev` link was forgotten.
With a doubly linked list, start `i` at the head and `j` at the tail and walk them toward each other, comparing values. Stop when they meet (odd length) or cross (even length).
A `list` has no `[]`. To reach index `X`, start at `l.begin()` and do `it++` X times; `next(it, k)` does the same in one call. `l.insert(it, v)` puts `v` before `it`; `l.erase(it)` removes it.
After `cin >> Q`, a newline is still waiting. Call `cin.ignore()` before the first `getline`, or the first line you read will be empty.

files.title: Q1 · Remove duplicates and sort (STL list)
files.what: Reads numbers until `-1` into a `list<int>`, then prints them sorted with every duplicate removed.
steps: Read values in a `while(true)` loop and `push_back` each one; stop at `-1`.
`l.sort()` puts equal values next to each other.
`l.unique()` deletes each value that equals the one just before it.
Print the list with a range-based `for`.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n) · Space O(n)
files.input_note: Values on one line, ending with `-1` (which is not part of the list).
files.watch_out: `unique()` without `sort()` only removes neighbouring copies: `1 2 1` would stay `1 2 1`.

check.a: `unique()` only removes consecutive equal elements; sorting makes all copies consecutive.

files.title: Q1 · Remove duplicates (practice copy)
files.what: Same solution; only the list is called `myList`.
steps: Read until `-1`, then `sort()`, `unique()` and print — identical to the original.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n) · Space O(n)
files.output_note: `10 20` — many copies of two values collapse to one each.

check.q: What would the output be for `3 -1`?
check.a: `3` — a single value is already sorted and unique.

files.title: Q2 · Insert at index X, print both ways
files.what: Starts with an empty doubly linked list. For each query `X V` it inserts `V` at index `X` (or prints `Invalid`) and then prints the list left-to-right and right-to-left.
steps: `get_size` counts the nodes so we know the valid range `0..size`.
If `pos < 0` or `pos > size`, print `Invalid` and stop this query.
`pos == 0` uses `insert_at_head`; `pos == size` uses `insert_at_tail`.
Otherwise walk `tmp` to the node at index `pos-1`.
Link the new node: `newNode->next = tmp->next`, `tmp->next->prev = newNode`, `tmp->next = newNode`, `newNode->prev = tmp`.
After each successful insert, `print_forward(head)` and `print_backward(tail)`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) per query · Space O(n)
files.output_note: The first query fails (`Invalid`, index 1 on an empty list). Then the list grows `10` → `10 20` → `5 10 20` → `5 7 10 20`; every `R ->` line is the exact mirror of the `L ->` line, which proves the `prev` links are right.
files.watch_out: The size check must allow `pos == size` (append at the end) but reject `pos > size`.

check.q: For the list `5 10 20`, which node does `tmp` stop on for query `2 99`?
check.a: The node at index 1 (`10`), because the loop runs `pos-1 = 1` step; `99` is linked right after it.

files.title: Q2 · Insert at index X (practice copy, has a bug)
files.what: Re-typed version of Q2, but `insert_at_head` was written with the tail-insert body, and the labels are `L -->`/`R -->`.
steps: Same size check, same middle insertion as the original.
**Difference:** `insert_at_head` links the new node after `tail` instead of before `head`.
Printing labels use `-->` instead of `->`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) per query · Space O(n)
files.input_note: Same input as the original, so you can compare.
files.output_note: Query `0 5` should give `5 10 20` but this prints `10 20 5` — the value went to the end. The next insert then lands in the wrong place too (`10 7 20 5`).
files.watch_out: Bug: `insert_at_head` must be `newNode->next = head; head->prev = newNode; head = newNode;`. Also the judge expects exactly `L -> ` and `R -> `, so the `-->` labels would fail.

check.q: Which line of output first shows the bug for this input?
check.a: `L --> 10 20 5` after query `0 5`: a head insert ended up at the tail.

files.title: Scratch: Q2 with STL list (does not compile)
files.what: An attempt to solve Q2 with `list<int>` and iterators: walk an iterator `X` steps and `l.insert(it, V)`, then print forward and backward.
steps: Reject `X < 0` or `X > size` with `Invalid`.
Move `it` from `l.begin()` forward `X` times.
`l.insert(it, V)` places `V` before `it` (at `l.end()` it appends).
`print_backward` starts at the last element with `next(l.begin(), l.size()-1)` and steps `it--` until `begin()`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) per query · Space O(n)
files.output_note: No output: the file fails to compile.
files.watch_out: Compile error: the function header is `void (list<int> &l, int X, int V)` — the name is missing. Fix: `void insert_at_any_position(list<int> &l, int X, int V)`.

check.q: Where does `l.insert(it, V)` put `V` when `it == l.end()`?
check.a: At the back of the list — inserting before `end()` is an append.

files.title: Q3 · Palindrome with a doubly linked list
files.what: Reads values until `-1` into a doubly linked list and checks whether it reads the same both ways, using one pointer from each end.
steps: Build the list with `insert_at_tail` so `head` and `tail` are both known.
Start `i = head`, `j = tail`.
Continue while `i != j` (odd length: they meet) and `i->prev != j` (even length: they crossed).
If `i->val != j->val`, set `flag = false` and stop.
Each round moves `i` to `next` and `j` to `prev`; print `YES` or `NO`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) for the list
files.output_note: `YES` — pairs (1,1), (2,2) match and the pointers meet at `3`.
files.watch_out: Both stop conditions are needed. With only `i != j`, an even-length list lets the pointers cross without ever being equal, so they keep walking until they fall off the ends and read `NULL` (crash).

check.q: For `1 2 2 1`, when does the loop stop?
check.a: After comparing (1,1) and (2,2), `i` is the second `2` and `j` is the first `2`, so `i->prev == j` and the loop ends.

files.title: Q3 · Palindrome (practice copy)
steps: Same two-pointer walk from `head` and `tail`.
files.output_note: `NO` — the second pair is (2, 3), which don't match.

check.q: Is a single value like `7 -1` a palindrome here?
check.a: Yes. `i == j` from the start, so the loop never runs and `flag` stays `true`.

files.title: Q4 · Browser history (visit / next / prev)
files.what: Stores web addresses in a `list<string>` and keeps the current address in `curr`. Commands move to a named address, the next one or the previous one, printing `Not Available` when the move is impossible.
steps: Read words until `end` into `Web`; read `Q` and call `cin.ignore()` so `getline` works.
Each query reads a full line and splits it with `stringstream` into `command` (and `address`).
`visit`: search the list; if found, set `*curr` and print it, else print `Not Available` and stay.
`next`: walk the list; the element right after the one equal to `*curr` becomes current. If none, `Not Available`.
`prev`: if `*curr` is the first element, `Not Available`; otherwise remember the last element seen before reaching `*curr` and move there.
`curr` is passed as `string*` so the function can change `main`'s variable.
files.complexity: Time O(n) per query · Space O(n)
files.input:
facebook google phitron youtube twitter end
8
visit phitron
prev
prev
prev
next
visit twitter
next
visit django
files.input_note: Addresses ending with `end`, then `Q`, then one command per line.
files.output_note: `phitron` → `google` → `facebook` → `Not Available` (already at the first) → `google` → `twitter` → `Not Available` (twitter is last) → `Not Available` (django isn't in the list).
files.watch_out: Searching by value works only because the addresses are unique. Keeping a `list<string>::iterator` as the current position would make `next`/`prev` O(1).

check.a: `cin >> Q` leaves the newline in the buffer; without `ignore()` the first `getline` would read an empty line and the first command would be lost.

files.what: Re-typed Q4, but the `prev` branch is missing `return` after printing `Not Available`.
steps: Same `visit` and `next` logic.
**Difference:** at the first address, `prev` prints `Not Available` and then keeps going into the loop, which prints the first address again.
files.complexity: Time O(n) per query · Space O(n)
files.input:
facebook google phitron youtube twitter end
8
visit phitron
prev
prev
prev
next
visit twitter
next
visit django
files.input_note: Same input as the original, for comparison.
files.output_note: Compare with the original: after `Not Available` an extra `facebook` line appears, so this prints 9 lines for 8 queries.
files.watch_out: Bug: add `return;` after `cout << "Not Available" << endl;` in the `prev` branch.

check.q: Why does the extra line say `facebook`?
check.a: The loop finds `*curr` (facebook) at the first element, where `prev` still holds `web.front()` — also facebook — so it prints that.

files.title: Q5 · Head / tail / delete queries (STL list)
files.what: Handles three query types on a `list<int>`: `0 V` push front, `1 V` push back, `2 V` erase index `V` if it exists. After every query the list is printed both ways.
steps: `X == 0` → `l.push_front(V)`; `X == 1` → `l.push_back(V)`.
`X == 2` → only if `0 <= V < l.size()`, move an iterator `V` steps and `l.erase(it)`.
`print_forward` walks from `begin()` to `end()`.
`print_backward` handles the empty list first, then starts at the last element and walks with `it--` until `begin()`.
Printing happens even if the delete was invalid.
files.complexity: Time O(n) per query · Space O(n)
files.output_note: After four inserts the list is `40 10 20 30`. `2 1` erases index 1 (`10`) giving `40 20 30`. `2 9` is out of range, so the same list is printed again.
files.watch_out: On an empty list, `next(l.begin(), l.size()-1)` would be invalid (`size()-1` wraps around), which is why `print_backward` checks `l.empty()` first. `l.rbegin()`..`l.rend()` is the simpler way to print backward.

files.title: Q5 · List queries (practice copy)
steps: Same three query types and the same two print functions.
files.complexity: Time O(n) per query · Space O(n)
files.output_note: `4` → `9 4` → erase index 0 → `4` → erase index 0 → empty list, shown as bare `L -> ` and `R -> ` lines.

check.q: Why does the empty list still print `L -> ` and `R -> `?
check.a: The labels are printed before checking for elements, so an empty list shows the labels with nothing after them — exactly what the problem asks.

recap: Valid insert indexes are `0..size`; the ends are special cases.
Print backward from `tail` to prove your `prev` links are correct.
Two pointers from both ends check a palindrome in one pass.

check_yourself.q: In a doubly linked list insert in the middle, which four pointers change?
How do you reach index `k` in an STL `list`?
check_yourself.a: Start at `begin()` and advance `k` times (`it++` or `next(l.begin(), k)`); there is no `[]` operator.

check_yourself.q: Why do the `_p` files deserve a careful diff against the originals?
check_yourself.a: Small re-typing slips (a wrong function body, a missing `return`) change the output while the code still compiles.
